Epicurus

Epicurus (c. 341–270 BCE) refined Democritean atomism and introduced a concept of striking relevance to Bayesian accounts of cognition: prolepsis, or preconception 1. A prolepsis is a general mental pattern formed from repeated sensory encounters—a kind of learned prior—that allows the mind to categorize and anticipate new experiences before full sensory evidence arrives. Perception, on this view, is never raw; it is always shaped by what the mind already expects.

Chrysippus

The Stoic philosopher Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BCE) developed a sophisticated theory of mental content centered on phantasia (impression or representation). Sensory impressions are stamped into the hegemonikon (ruling faculty), which Chrysippus located in the brain. Crucially, not every impression compels belief: the mind must give synkatathesis (assent) to an impression before it becomes a commitment about the world. This two-stage architecture—automatic sensory representation followed by evaluative acceptance—prefigures modern dual-process theories and the distinction between perceptual inference and decision.

Lucretius

Lucretius (c. 99–55 BCE) rendered Epicurean physics into Latin verse in De Rerum Natura 2, producing the most detailed surviving ancient account of materialist perception. Simulacra—films of atoms continually shed by objects—enter the sense organs and produce experience through physical impact. Thought, dreaming, and hallucination arise from residual or recombined simulacra, establishing a single mechanistic framework for veridical and non-veridical experience alike.

Galen

Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 CE) transformed the study of the brain from speculation into experimental science 3, 4. Through systematic dissection and vivisection of animals, he traced cranial nerves, identified the cerebrum and cerebellum as functionally distinct, and demonstrated—by ligating nerves and compressing brain regions—that the brain controls sensation and voluntary movement. His ventricular doctrine, which localized perception, reasoning, and memory to the fluid-filled cerebral ventricles, would dominate neuroscience for over a thousand years.

Augustine

Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE) turned philosophical attention inward. Book X of the Confessions 5 contains an extraordinary phenomenology of memory: a “vast palace” of stored experiences that the mind can search, recombine, and deploy in the production of expectations. His analysis of time perception in Book XI—where the present is a vanishing knife-edge between expectatio (anticipation of what is coming) and memoria (retention of what has passed)—describes the temporal structure of experience in terms strikingly compatible with predictive processing: the mind lives perpetually in the gap between prediction and recollection.

Sextus Empiricus

Sextus Empiricus (c. 160–210 CE) compiled the most systematic surviving statement of Pyrrhonian skepticism 6, 7. His ten modes (tropoi) demonstrate that every perception is relative—to the species of the perceiver, to the individual, to the sense organ, to the circumstances, to the position and distance, to the admixtures, to the quantity and composition, to the frequency of encounter, and to the cultural context. Since one can never step outside perception to compare a representation with how things “really are,” one ought to suspend judgment (epochē) about the nature of external reality. For world-modeling neuroscience, Sextus articulates in philosophical terms the fundamental epistemic predicament of any brain: locked behind its sensory surfaces, a brain has access only to its own representations, never to the world those representations purport to describe—a predicament later formalized as the “evidentiary boundary” of the Markov blanket.

Plotinus

Plotinus (c. 204–270 CE), the founder of Neoplatonism, described reality as a cascade of emanations from a unitary source: the One gives rise to Nous (Intellect), which gives rise to Psychē (Soul), which gives rise to the material world [Enneads]. Consciousness occupies an intermediary position, oriented simultaneously toward the intelligible realm and the sensible realm below. Most remarkably for present purposes, Plotinus argued that the soul does not passively receive sensory impressions but actively generates its own awareness: external objects are occasions for the soul’s activity, not causes of its states. This top-down, generative picture of awareness—in which the mind’s own productive activity takes priority over bottom-up sensory input—has a strikingly modern resonance with hierarchical predictive models in which perception is driven more by descending predictions than ascending signals.
